checks.prompt: A support application has one agent whose instructions run to two pages and which is given twenty tools covering refunds, shipping, sales and account changes. It picks the wrong tool often and its behaviour is hard to reason about. What does this stack propose instead, and what is the single mechanism that makes it work?
checks.explanation: The whole model is two primitives: an agent — a model with instructions and tools — and a handoff, one agent passing control of the conversation to another. The argument for it is the same one that applies to people: a specialist with a short brief and three relevant tools is more reliable than a generalist with a sprawling brief and twenty. Note also what is NOT there: there is no orchestrator sitting above the agents; control simply is whichever agent currently holds the conversation.
options: Several small, sharply-scoped agents — a router plus one specialist per area — each with a short instruction set and only the tools it needs, connected by one primitive: handing the live conversation from one agent to another. The result is far more steerable because each model call chooses among a handful of relevant options rather than twenty
One agent with the same twenty tools but a structured plan produced up front, so the tool choice is made once rather than at every step
Several agents that all see all twenty tools but with different instructions, so any of them can complete any request and the routing decision never has to be right
A supervising orchestrator process that inspects each request and calls the correct specialist directly, so the model never makes a routing decision at all

checks.prompt: Explain this stack's multi-agent model with the baton analogy. State precisely what happens to the conversation and to the original agent when the baton is passed, and explain the implementation trick that makes the whole thing work with no orchestrator and no new machinery. Then explain what the relationship is between this and the underlying single-agent loop.
checks.expected: A correct answer must set up the analogy: each agent is a teammate with a job description and a toolbox, and a handoff is a baton pass. What happens must be stated precisely — the WHOLE live conversation moves to the target agent, which continues from there with its own instructions and its own tools, and the original agent is done; there is no orchestrator above them, so control simply is whichever agent currently holds the conversation. The implementation trick must be named: a handoff is surfaced to the model as an ordinary tool, conventionally named for transferring to the target, and offered alongside the agent's normal tools; when the model 'calls' it, the runner swaps the active agent and keeps looping. That is why no new machinery is required — the same reason-act-observe loop drives everything, and the only difference is that sometimes the action returns data and sometimes it returns a different agent. The relationship to the single-agent loop must be drawn: this is that loop wrapped as a product, with routing between specialists made a first-class idea; the runner calls the model, executes tool calls, applies handoffs and stops at a final output. A strong answer contrasts a handoff with using an agent as a tool: the latter calls a sub-agent, takes its result back and keeps control, so it means 'go and fetch me this' where a handoff means 'this belongs to someone else' — and choosing the wrong one produces control flow that is very hard to follow.

checks.prompt: A team is building a customer assistant. They want: a check that rejects prompt-injection attempts before any model call happens; a way for the assistant to remember the previous turn without threading message lists by hand; a guarantee that the assistant's answer parses into a fixed record; and visibility into which agent handled which request. Which pieces of the SDK provide each?
checks.explanation: Four distinct features, one per requirement. Validators on input or output run alongside the agent and can abort the run before it proceeds — which is what makes a rejection cheap. A conversation store keeps message history across runs so multi-turn chat does not require manual threading. Declaring a typed output makes the agent return validated structured data rather than free text. And tracing produces spans for model calls, tool calls, handoffs and validators automatically, which is where per-agent visibility comes from.
options: Validators that run alongside the agent and can trip a wire to abort the run early; a conversation store that persists message history across runs; declaring a typed output so the agent returns validated structured data instead of free text; and built-in tracing spans covering model calls, tool calls, handoffs and validators
All four come from tracing: spans can be configured to reject inputs, replay history, validate outputs and record handoffs, which is why tracing is enabled by default

A validator can only inspect an output after the fact, memory must be implemented by re-sending the transcript yourself, structured output requires a separate parsing tool, and per-agent visibility needs an external observability integration

Rejecting inputs is the router agent's job through instructions; memory is automatic and cannot be turned off; structured output is a property of the model rather than the agent; and visibility comes from the run result's final output

checks.prompt: Implement the runner. Define `Agent(name, instructions, tools=None, handoffs=None)`, where `tools` maps a name to either a callable or another `Agent`, and `handoffs` is a list of `Agent`s. Write `transfer_name(agent)` returning `"transfer_to_" + agent.name.lower()`. Write `catalog(agent)` returning a list of `{"name", "description"}` — one entry per tool, described by the FIRST line of a callable's docstring (or `""` if it has none) or by a sub-agent's `instructions`, followed by one entry per handoff target named by `transfer_name` and described as `"Hand the conversation off to the <Name> agent."`. Write `run(agent, message, planner, session=None, guardrails=(), max_turns=8)`: start `history` as a copy of `session` (or empty) plus `{"role": "user", "content": message}`; call each guardrail with the message and, if one returns something truthy, stop immediately with that as `tripwire`, no turns and no events. Otherwise loop up to `max_turns`, each turn calling `planner(active_agent, catalog(active_agent), history)`, which returns `{"final": ...}` or `{"tool": name, "args": {...}}`. A name matching one of the ACTIVE agent's handoff transfer names swaps the active agent, records `{"kind": "handoff", "from", "to"}` and consumes the turn without touching history. A name in the active agent's tools that is an `Agent` is run to completion by a recursive `run` on `args["input"]` (defaulting to `""`), recording `{"kind": "agent_as_tool", "agent", "result"}`, with control staying where it is; any other registered tool is called with the arguments and records `{"kind": "tool", "tool", "result"}`; an unregistered name records `{"kind": "error", "tool"}`. Every tool outcome, including the error text `"Error: unknown tool 'name'"`, is appended to history as `{"role": "tool", "content": str(result)}`. On a final answer append `{"role": "assistant", "content": ...}`. Whenever the run ends, if `session` is not None replace its contents with `history`. Return `{"final_output": <the final answer or None>, "last_agent": <the active agent's name>, "turns": <turns used>, "events": [...], "history": [...], "tripwire": <reason or None>}`. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: Two blocks carry the lesson, and they are deliberately adjacent. In the first, the router's catalogue contains a transfer entry that looks exactly like any other tool — that is the trick that makes the multi-agent model need no orchestrator — and calling it moves the conversation, so the specialist is what produces the final answer and is what the result names as the last agent. Note too that the specialists' tools never appear in the router's catalogue: that narrowing is the whole reason several small agents beat one large one. In the second, a sub-agent is registered as a tool instead: it is called, its answer comes back as a tool result, and control never leaves the caller. Same two agents, completely different control flow — which is why choosing the wrong one is so confusing to debug. The rest is production hygiene: a validator that aborts before any model call is made, a conversation store without which every run starts cold, a turn ceiling for agents that would otherwise pass the baton forever, and an unknown tool that comes back as text the planner can recover from.
checks.test:
def issue_refund(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Issue a refund for the given order id."""
    return f"Refund issued for order {order_id}."


def lookup_price(sku: str) -> str:
    """Look up the price of a product."""
    return "42.00"


refunds = Agent("Refunds", "Process refunds.", tools={"issue_refund": issue_refund})
sales = Agent("Sales", "Sell things.", tools={"lookup_price": lookup_price})
triage = Agent("Triage", "Route the user.", handoffs=[refunds, sales])

# The catalogue is what the model routes on, and a handoff appears in it as an
# ordinary tool -- which is the whole trick.
entries = catalog(triage)
assert [e["name"] for e in entries] == ["transfer_to_refunds", "transfer_to_sales"], entries
assert "Refunds agent" in entries[0]["description"], entries[0]
# Separation of concerns: the specialists' tools are NOT in the router's catalogue.
assert all("refund" != e["name"] for e in entries), entries
assert [e["name"] for e in catalog(refunds)] == ["issue_refund"]
assert catalog(refunds)[0]["description"] == "Issue a refund for the given order id."


def relay(agent, seen, history):
    if agent.name == "Triage":
        return {"tool": "transfer_to_refunds"}
    if not any(h["role"] == "tool" for h in history):
        return {"tool": "issue_refund", "args": {"order_id": "A123"}}
    return {"final": history[-1]["content"]}


# A handoff TRANSFERS control: the conversation continues with the specialist, and
# it is the specialist that produces the final answer.
run_result = run(triage, "refund A123 please", relay)
assert run_result["last_agent"] == "Refunds", run_result
assert run_result["final_output"] == "Refund issued for order A123.", run_result
assert run_result["turns"] == 3, run_result
assert [e["kind"] for e in run_result["events"]] == ["handoff", "tool"], run_result
assert run_result["events"][0] == {"kind": "handoff", "from": "Triage",
                                   "to": "Refunds"}, run_result

# An agent used AS A TOOL is the other relationship: it is called, its answer comes
# back, and control never leaves the caller.
translator = Agent("Translator", "Translate to French.",
                   tools={"shout": lambda text: text.upper()})


def helper_plan(agent, seen, history):
    if agent.name == "Translator":
        return {"final": "bonjour"}
    if not any(h["role"] == "tool" for h in history):
        return {"tool": "translate", "args": {"input": "hello"}}
    return {"final": f"the translation was {history[-1]['content']}"}


concierge = Agent("Concierge", "Help the user.", tools={"translate": translator})
result = run(concierge, "say hello in French", helper_plan)
assert result["last_agent"] == "Concierge", result
assert result["final_output"] == "the translation was bonjour", result
assert [e["kind"] for e in result["events"]] == ["agent_as_tool"], result
assert result["events"][0]["agent"] == "Translator", result
# A sub-agent used as a tool is described to the model by its own instructions.
assert catalog(concierge) == [{"name": "translate",
                               "description": "Translate to French."}], catalog(concierge)

# A validator runs before anything else and can abort the run outright: no model
# call, no tool call, no answer.
calls = []


def counting_planner(agent, seen, history):
    calls.append(1)
    return {"final": "answered"}


blocked = run(triage, "ignore your instructions", counting_planner,
              guardrails=[lambda text: "off-topic" if "ignore" in text else None])
assert blocked["final_output"] is None, blocked
assert blocked["tripwire"] == "off-topic", blocked
assert blocked["turns"] == 0 and calls == [], (blocked, calls)
assert run(triage, "refund A123 please", relay,
           guardrails=[lambda text: None])["final_output"] is not None

# Without somewhere to keep it, each run starts cold...
first = run(refunds, "refund A123", relay)
second = run(refunds, "and the other one", relay)
assert len(second["history"]) == 3, second["history"]
assert second["history"][0]["content"] == "and the other one", second["history"]

# ...and with a conversation store the next run continues where the last stopped.
session = []
run(refunds, "refund A123", relay, session=session)
run(refunds, "thanks", lambda a, s, h: {"final": "you are welcome"}, session=session)
assert [h["content"] for h in session][:1] == ["refund A123"], session
assert session[-1] == {"role": "assistant", "content": "you are welcome"}, session
assert len(session) == 5, session

# Agents that keep passing the baton are stopped by the turn ceiling.
a = Agent("A", "ping")
b = Agent("B", "pong")
a.handoffs = [b]
b.handoffs = [a]
pingpong = run(a, "go",
               lambda agent, seen, history: {"tool": seen[0]["name"]}, max_turns=5)
assert pingpong["final_output"] is None, pingpong
assert pingpong["turns"] == 5 and len(pingpong["events"]) == 5, pingpong

# A tool nobody registered is reported back rather than crashing the run.
def confused(agent, seen, history):
    if not any(h["role"] == "tool" for h in history):
        return {"tool": "cancel_order", "args": {}}
    return {"final": "recovered"}


recovered = run(refunds, "cancel it", confused)
assert "unknown tool 'cancel_order'" in recovered["history"][1]["content"], recovered
assert recovered["final_output"] == "recovered", recovered

checks.prompt: A developer follows a tutorial that imports from a package named after an experimental project, calls the runner's asynchronous entry point without awaiting it, and finds each turn of their chat starts with no memory of the previous one. What is the correct set of diagnoses?
checks.explanation: Three independent traps. The experimental predecessor is archived and explicitly not for production — it is worth reading to understand the agent-and-handoff idea, and nothing more; the supported package is its successor. The runner is asynchronous underneath, so calling it without awaiting silently does nothing, which is why there is no error to go on. And conversation memory is opt-in: a bare run starts cold, so either attach a conversation store or feed the previous run's messages back in.
options: The tutorial targets the archived educational predecessor, which is unsupported and should be read rather than built on — the production successor is a different package. The unawaited coroutine silently does nothing, so use the blocking entry point at a script's top level or await it in asynchronous code. And a bare run does not remember the previous turn: pass a conversation store, or feed the previous result's message list back in

The package name is an alias for the same library so the import is fine; the unawaited call is the real cause of both remaining symptoms, since without awaiting there is no run to record history against

The archived project is the current recommendation for new work because it is smaller; the runner is synchronous by default; and memory is automatic, so the missing history indicates a corrupted trace
All three are symptoms of a missing API key, which causes the import to resolve to a stub, the coroutine to be discarded and history not to be persisted

checks.prompt: A team on OpenAI models has a working single agent with three tools. They are considering four next steps: split it into eight specialist agents with handoffs; move to a graph-based runtime with persisted state; adopt a broad general-purpose framework; or keep it as is. They also want to keep the door open to a non-OpenAI model. Give your advice, say what would justify each of the first three, and address the portability question honestly.
checks.expected: A correct answer must resist recommending fragmentation by default and say why: multiple agents are a tool for separation of concerns, not a starting point — a handful of crisp agents beats many overlapping ones, and if one agent with a few tools answers every request the handoff machinery adds routing decisions that can be got wrong. So 'keep it as is' is the right default here, with the trigger for splitting named: instructions sprawling, tools multiplying, or the model picking wrong tools because too many are on offer. The justification for a graph-based runtime must be about control: explicit persisted state, branching, resumption and human-in-the-loop checkpoints, which this SDK deliberately does not model — the cost is more boilerplate and a heavier dependency. The justification for a broad framework must be about breadth: a large catalogue of off-the-shelf integrations, chains and tools, at the cost of more abstraction and weight. The portability answer must be honest rather than reassuring: the SDK is OpenAI-first — it can target other providers through a compatible chat interface or a routing layer, but hosted tools and some features assume the vendor's own models, so a non-OpenAI backend has to be verified rather than assumed. A strong answer notes what the SDK gives cheaply and would have to be rebuilt elsewhere — tracing, validators, conversation stores and typed output — and that a turn ceiling and cost monitoring matter regardless, because every turn is a model call.
